title: Atlas and Uniform
premise: In the winter of 1917, Wendell Delacroix works as a battlefield nurse near a frozen river on the eastern edge of the war, keeping a private ledger of soldiers whose names officers omit from official records. When a stranger arrives bearing letters in handwriting identical to that of Lieutenant Emile Vasseur—a man officially declared dead, and now listed among the enemy—Wendell is forced to confront the promise she made to Emile in peacetime: that if he ever vanished, she would carry his true name home. As suspicion falls on her for harboring enemy correspondence, she must choose between the safety of invisibility and the dangerous act of witness, delivering the ledger and the letters across the ice before the spring thaw destroys both the river crossing and her last chance. The novel ends with Wendell testifying before a postwar commission, reading names aloud until the room understands that history was never happening elsewhere—it was happening to her all along.
about_author: Vesper Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from European field hospitals. Atlas and Uniform is their first novel, drawn from the marginalia of ledgers no one thought worth saving.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Hours
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In a freezing field hospital, Wendell tends the wounded by night and records omitted names in her hidden ledger by candlelight, convinced she is merely a bystander to history. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: she believes naming the unnamed is enough, and that staying unseen keeps her safe.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A mud-caked stranger arrives at the checkpoint carrying a satchel he refuses to open, asking for 'the one who writes.' He slips Wendell a letter in handwriting she knows intimately—Emile Vasseur's, a man three months dead by official record. The beat is vertigo: her careful distance collapses in a single sentence.

chapters.title: What We Promised in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with flashback chapters of memory woven through. She recalls the summer before the war: Emile's laughter, his fear of being erased by his family's name, and the promise she made—that if he disappeared, she would make sure someone knew who he truly was. The beat is tender grief sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Enemy's Hand
chapters.summary: Major Aldous Renwick's POV. Renwick intercepts word of unauthorized correspondence and begins quietly investigating the hospital staff, suspecting a spy ring. He notices Wendell's steady competence and finds it suspicious rather than admirable. The beat is cold dread from the outside: we see how easily her invisibility can be reframed as guilt.

chapters.title: Ice Over the River
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The stranger reveals Emile is alive—defected, declared enemy, trapped on the far bank—and asks her to bring the ledger across the ice so Emile can verify the names before witnesses arrive. Wendell refuses at first, terrified. The beat is the cost of belonging: helping means becoming visible, visible means punishable.

chapters.title: Names That Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A mass casualty wave floods the ward; Renwick orders records burned to simplify reporting. Wendell watches men become statistics in real time and copies names faster than the fire can take them. The beat is fury transmuted into purpose—she will cross the ice not for Emile alone, but for every name in the book.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Satchel
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Wendell and the stranger, Tomas, who confesses he is Emile's brother-in-arms sent to test whether the promise would be kept—or whether it was sentiment. Wendell learns the letters are partly forged bait set by Renwick to draw out collaborators. The beat is betrayal and recalibration: trust must be rebuilt on evidence, not affection.

chapters.title: Before the Thaw
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. With Renwick closing in and the ice thinning, Wendell makes her decision at nightfall: she takes the ledger, the true letter, and crosses the frozen river alone. Midway, the ice groans and cracks; she nearly loses the satchel and nearly turns back. The beat is terror transformed into commitment—the point of no return.

chapters.title: The Far Bank
chapters.summary: Emile's POV. On the enemy side, Wendell finds Emile alive but broken, ashamed of his uniform and certain his name deserves erasure. She reads him the ledger aloud, name after name, refusing to let him renounce himself. The beat is the climax's emotional core: identity cannot be surrendered, only witnessed. They seal the record together as dawn breaks.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, two years later. Before a postwar commission, Renwick's accusations dissolved and the war ended, Wendell stands as the ledger's custodian and reads the names into the official record while Emile watches from the gallery. The beat is resolution and inheritance: history happened here, to us, and now it belongs to everyone who hears it.
